subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: Rafiq sits across from me at the consulting firm, so I have watched him for two years. On client calls his English is polished, precise, slightly formal. Ten minutes later he is on the phone with his mother, and it's Dakhni with a loud laugh that makes the whole row smile. He keeps a small notebook of Dakhni proverbs from his mother and reads one to his nephew on video every Sunday. I can't say for sure whether he ever feels fake when he switches. He doesn't look it; he looks like a man using the right tool for the right job. Once I asked him. He said, "The English gets me work. The Dakhni keeps me whole." Anand

qa.q: What does Rafiq keep in a small notebook?
qa.a: Rafiq keeps a small notebook of Dakhni proverbs from his mother.

qa.q: What does Rafiq's answer suggest he feels about switching between the two ways of speaking?
qa.a: He seems comfortable and settled, and does not feel fake. He treats English as the tool for work and Dakhni as what keeps him whole.

qa.q: Which choice by Rafiq keeps his mother tongue alive?
qa.a: Rafiq writes down his mother's Dakhni proverbs and reads one to his nephew on video every Sunday.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's mother feel when he laughs with her on the phone?
qa.a: Probably happy and close, since his Dakhni keeps them connected.

grounding: A young adult moves between casual home speech and polished professional English without feeling fake and keeps the mother tongue alive.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: Monday. In his first week at a Bengaluru software firm, Harish rehearsed every sentence in polished English and felt like a fraud. That evening he spoke Kannada with his mother on the phone and relaxed at once, and felt guilty about the difference. Wednesday. His senior colleague Pradeep, hearing him practise, said, "You're not being fake. You're switching tools. My grandmother's Tulu and my client English are both mine." Harish laughed, surprised. Saturday. Harish ran a client call in clear English without rehearsing. Afterwards he taught his cousin a Kannada tongue-twister on video and laughed until he coughed. He felt like the same person both times.

qa.q: What did Pradeep say about switching?
qa.a: Pradeep said, "You're not being fake. You're switching tools."

qa.q: How did Harish feel on Monday about his rehearsed English?
qa.a: Harish felt like a fraud and a little guilty about how different he sounded at home.

qa.q: What turning point on Wednesday changed how Harish saw his two ways of speaking?
qa.a: Pradeep told him it was switching tools, not being fake, and gave his own example of Tulu and client English, so Harish stopped seeing one as false.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Harish's worry?
qa.a: As familiar, since Pradeep also moves between a grandmother's Tulu and client English and calls both his own.

grounding: A young adult moves between casual home speech and polished professional English without feeling fake and sees each register as a tool.
